cardVisual.title: A name anchors the subject
cardVisual.caption: An identifier names a subject; evidence and policy answer different questions.

blocks.title: From claim to accountable subject
blocks.caption: The record gives later controls a stable subject to evaluate.

items.label: Claim
items.detail: A person, device, process, or service says who it is.

items.label: Bind
items.detail: Registration links the identifier to an owned record.

items.label: Record assurance
items.detail: Source, owner, evidence, and review date make confidence inspectable.

blocks.title: Three questions, three jobs
blocks.caption: Keeping these questions separate prevents a directory entry from becoming permission.

blocks.prompt: What does an identifier do?
options: It proves the claimant controls the account
It grants access to every resource
blocks.explanation: An identifier names the subject. Authentication supplies evidence and authorization evaluates the requested action.
blocks.hint: A label is not evidence.

blocks.prompt: Which record most improves accountability for a service identity?
options: An owner, purpose, environment, and review date
A list of every possible permission
blocks.explanation: Non-human identities need an accountable owner and context so their use and access can be reviewed.
blocks.hint: Ask who owns the identity and why it exists.

blocks.prompt: A user logs in successfully but receives a file denial. Which distinction explains this?
options: Authentication succeeded but authorization denied the action
blocks.explanation: Successful authentication establishes control of an identity; authorization still decides whether this subject may perform this action on this object.
blocks.hint: Separate proof of control from permission.

leadVisual.title: Three questions. Three different jobs.
leadVisual.caption: Naming an identity does not prove the claim. Proving the claim does not grant every permission.

cardVisual.title: Two steps are not always two factors
cardVisual.caption: Different screens do not create independent evidence.

items.label: Password + PIN
items.detail: Two knowledge secrets · one factor category

blocks.title: Count independent categories
blocks.caption: Two prompts are not automatically two factors; compromise of one category should not defeat both.

blocks.title: Assurance continues after login
blocks.caption: A successful authenticator check starts a session; it does not make the session permanent.

items.label: Authenticate
items.detail: Verify the authenticator and create an event.

items.label: Use session
items.detail: Apply bounded lifetime and anti-hijacking controls.

items.label: Recheck or revoke
items.detail: Respond to elapsed time, risk, logout, or compromise.

blocks.prompt: Which pair uses independent factor categories?
blocks.explanation: A password is knowledge and a security key is possession. Two passwords remain one category.
blocks.hint: Classify each item as know, have, or are.

blocks.prompt: Why should recovery be designed with the primary authenticator?
options: A weak reset path can bypass a strong login
Recovery removes the need for authorization
blocks.explanation: An attacker may target account recovery instead of the primary authenticator, so the recovery path must match the intended assurance.
blocks.hint: Find the alternate route into the account.

blocks.prompt: What does authentication establish for a new session?
options: Evidence that the claimant controls an associated authenticator
That the user owns the resource
blocks.explanation: Authentication verifies control of an authenticator; authorization and session policy still govern what happens next.
blocks.hint: It answers “who controls the authenticator?”

leadVisual.title: Count the factors, not the steps.
leadVisual.caption: Password + PIN = one factor category. A device-bound authenticator unlocked with a biometric can combine possession and inherence; biometrics are not a standalone remote authenticator.

cardVisual.title: Signed in ≠ allowed
cardVisual.caption: Authorization evaluates the request in context and enforces the resulting permit or deny.

blocks.title: A policy decision needs the whole request
blocks.caption: “Logged in” omits the details that make an authorization decision defensible.

items.label: Context
items.detail: Device, time, location, status, or purpose

blocks.title: Separate decision from enforcement
blocks.caption: A correct rule still fails if an enforcement boundary ignores or misapplies its result.

items.label: Policy enforcement point
items.detail: Applies the result at the API or resource boundary.

items.label: Decision record
items.detail: Captures policy version and relevant context.

blocks.prompt: Which request is most useful to an authorization policy?
options: Morgan reads the assigned chart from a managed device during a shift
blocks.explanation: The useful request identifies subject, object, action, and relevant context.
blocks.hint: Look for more than identity or login state.

blocks.prompt: What is the enforcement point responsible for?
options: Applying the policy decision at the resource boundary
blocks.explanation: The enforcement point applies the decision at an API, application, database, operating system, or network boundary.
blocks.hint: It is where the result takes effect.

blocks.prompt: Why might a long-lived access token be unsafe after a role change?
options: The token may rely on stale authorization context
The identity record becomes a password
Role changes always invalidate authentication proof
blocks.explanation: A role or device condition can change while a token remains valid, so high-impact actions may need a fresh authorization decision.
blocks.hint: Ask whether the decision inputs are still current.

leadVisual.title: A request becomes a policy decision
leadVisual.caption: An authenticated session supplies context. The enforcement point still checks the requested action.

cardVisual.title: Who controls the permission?
cardVisual.caption: RBAC, ABAC, DAC, and MAC differ by policy inputs and decision authority.

blocks.title: The policy authority changes the model
blocks.caption: Identify who may grant or override access before naming the model.

items.label: RBAC
items.detail: A role carries permissions for a function.

items.label: DAC
items.detail: An owner or delegated controller may share an object.

items.label: MAC
items.detail: Central labels and rules constrain owners and users.

blocks.title: Combine a baseline with context
blocks.caption: A role can establish a baseline while attributes narrow the decision for this request.

items.label: Decision
items.detail: Permit only when the required conditions align

blocks.prompt: Which design best illustrates ABAC?
options: Every nurse gets the same fixed role permissions
A payroll role may edit only from a managed device during work hours
A file owner shares the document with a colleague
A central label blocks an uncleared user
blocks.explanation: ABAC evaluates attributes and conditions such as role, device posture, and time.
blocks.hint: Look for more than a role alone.

blocks.prompt: What distinguishes DAC from MAC?
options: DAC lets an owner exercise discretion; MAC uses centrally enforced policy
MAC is always based on job roles
blocks.explanation: DAC gives an owner or delegated controller discretion; MAC prevents a user from overriding the central rule simply by owning the object.
blocks.hint: Ask who has authority to share or override.

blocks.prompt: Why can a risk-based rule need a defined fallback?
options: A missing signal still needs an accountable response
A fallback makes every request permit
blocks.explanation: If a device-health or location signal is missing, the policy must say whether to block, step up, or handle the request another way.
blocks.hint: Consider what happens when an input is unavailable.

leadVisual.title: Same person. Different policy.

RBAC.policy: Only the Payroll role may edit salary records.
RBAC.reason: The permission comes from Morgan’s role.

ABAC.policy: Payroll staff may edit only from a managed device during work hours.
ABAC.input: Role: Payroll · Device: unmanaged · Time: 10 am
ABAC.reason: The role matches, but the device attribute fails the policy.

DAC.policy: The document owner may choose who receives edit access.
DAC.input: Owner shares the file with Morgan as an editor.
DAC.reason: The owner exercises discretion to grant the permission.

MAC.policy: A central policy requires the right clearance and approved need-to-know.
MAC.reason: The owner cannot override the mandatory policy.

leadVisual.caption: These examples isolate each model; real systems can combine them.

cardVisual.title: Enough power for the task
cardVisual.caption: Narrow grants and controlled elevation reduce the blast radius of mistakes and compromise.

blocks.title: Translate the task into a grant
blocks.caption: The grant should name the resource, operation, purpose, and duration rather than the person's seniority.

blocks.title: Make exceptional power temporary
blocks.caption: Just-in-time and break-glass paths make elevation deliberate and observable.

items.label: Approve
items.detail: Require appropriate approval or emergency criteria.

items.label: Expire and review
items.detail: Remove access and inspect its use.

blocks.prompt: Which grant best follows least privilege for a reporting service?
options: Read a reporting view with no production writes
blocks.explanation: The grant is sufficient for the task and excludes unrelated operations.
blocks.hint: Match the permission to the actual function.

blocks.prompt: What makes just-in-time elevation safer than standing admin access?
options: It limits elevated access to an approved task and period
It removes the need for logging
It gives every operator the same rights
blocks.explanation: Time-bounded elevation reduces the amount of standing privilege available to misuse or compromise.
blocks.hint: Focus on duration and purpose.

blocks.prompt: Why do permissions need recurring review?
options: Projects and responsibilities change, leaving stale grants
blocks.explanation: Access accumulates as people, systems, and projects change; review removes grants that no longer serve a current function.
blocks.hint: Least privilege can decay over time.

leadVisual.title: The smallest permission that gets the job done
leadVisual.caption: A reporting task needs read access to relevant data. It does not need the ability to edit production records.

cardVisual.title: A trusted assertion crosses the boundary
cardVisual.caption: The identity provider authenticates; the relying party validates, creates a session, and still applies local authorization.

items.label: Assertion
items.detail: Signed claim for a specific recipient

blocks.title: Three parties, separate responsibilities
blocks.caption: Federation reduces duplicate credentials but creates explicit trust and dependency boundaries.

items.label: Subscriber
items.detail: Person or service seeking the relying party.

items.label: Relying party
items.detail: Consumes the assertion and establishes local access.

blocks.title: Validate before creating the session
blocks.caption: Issuer, audience, signature, time, and transaction checks connect trust to the correct application.

items.label: Issuer
items.detail: Is this the provider we trust?

items.label: Audience
items.detail: Was this assertion intended for us?

items.label: Integrity and time
items.detail: Signature, expiry, nonce, and state are valid.

items.label: Local session
items.detail: Only then establish local access context.

blocks.prompt: What does the identity provider do in a typical federation flow?
options: Authenticates the subscriber and issues an assertion
blocks.explanation: The IdP authenticates and asserts; the relying party validates the assertion and makes local access decisions.
blocks.hint: Separate authentication from resource policy.

blocks.prompt: Why is an OAuth access token not automatically generic proof of user identity?
options: OAuth delegates API authorization; identity claims require the appropriate identity layer
An access token cannot have an audience
blocks.explanation: OAuth primarily delegates authorization to an API. OpenID Connect adds identity and authentication claims with their own validation rules.
blocks.hint: Ask what the token was designed to authorize.

blocks.prompt: What should a relying party do after accepting a valid assertion?
options: Create a local session and apply local authorization
Forward the user's password to each service
blocks.explanation: A valid assertion supports the authentication event; local policy still controls the requested resource and action.
blocks.hint: Federation crosses an identity boundary, not every permission boundary.

leadVisual.title: One trusted identity, another application
leadVisual.caption: The application trusts a validated assertion—not a forwarded password. Local authorization still applies.

cardVisual.title: Access follows the relationship
cardVisual.caption: Joiner, mover, and leaver events change access; a mover requires removal as well as addition.

blocks.title: A relationship event drives a control change
blocks.caption: The authoritative source and an accountable workflow keep access aligned with current work.

items.label: Source event
items.detail: HR, contract, device, or service ownership changes.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Confirm the new function and minimum need.

items.label: Change access
items.detail: Add, replace, suspend, or revoke grants.

blocks.title: A mover needs a subtraction
blocks.caption: Adding the new role without removing the old one creates accumulated access.

items.label: Old role
items.detail: Remove grants tied to the previous function.

blocks.prompt: What is the key access task for a joiner?
options: Copy every permission from a peer
Keep access undefined until the first incident
blocks.explanation: Joiner provisioning should start with the access needed for the approved function and no broader.
blocks.hint: Joiners need a baseline, not a permission dump.

blocks.prompt: Why is a mover an access removal event too?
options: Old grants may remain valid after the function changes
blocks.explanation: If old grants are not removed, the user accumulates permissions unrelated to the new role.
blocks.hint: Consider what happens to the old role.

blocks.prompt: Which response best fits a leaver event?
options: Revoke accounts, active sessions, and relevant credentials
Leave tokens active until their natural expiry
Archive the identity but keep all access
blocks.explanation: Termination should revoke usable access and sessions promptly, with evidence of the change.
blocks.hint: Leaver controls close active paths, not just the directory record.

leadVisual.title: Access follows the relationship
leadVisual.caption: A transfer is a removal event as well as an addition. Otherwise, permissions accumulate.

cardVisual.title: Make an action traceable
cardVisual.caption: Unique identity, protected records, and review connect an event to a responsible actor.

blocks.title: From actor to evidence
blocks.caption: Logging is useful only when the identity and record support a defensible attribution.

items.label: Unique identity
items.detail: A person or service can be distinguished.

items.label: Event fields
items.detail: Action, object, time, location, and outcome.

items.label: Protected record
items.detail: Integrity, access control, retention, and review.

blocks.title: A shared account breaks attribution
blocks.caption: A complete log can still fail to identify the human who acted if credentials are shared.

items.label: Shared credential
items.detail: The log names one account for many people.

items.label: Unique credential
items.detail: The event maps to an accountable subject.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Investigators can ask who, what, when, and why.

blocks.prompt: Which field most directly supports reconstructing an action?
options: Action, object, time, location, and outcome
blocks.explanation: Useful event records capture enough context to reconstruct what occurred and its result.
blocks.hint: Think like an investigator replaying the event.

blocks.prompt: What is the main accountability problem with a shared administrator account?
options: The event cannot reliably identify which person acted
blocks.explanation: A shared credential may produce a log entry but does not establish which individual performed the action.
blocks.hint: Ask who can be held responsible.

blocks.prompt: Why protect audit records after creating them?
options: Tampering or unauthorized access could undermine their evidentiary value
Protection turns every event into authentication
Protected logs no longer need timestamps
Review is unnecessary once a log exists
blocks.explanation: Integrity, access control, retention, and review keep records trustworthy enough for investigation.
blocks.hint: Evidence must remain credible after collection.

leadVisual.title: Make the action traceable
leadVisual.caption: Shared credentials weaken attribution. Logging alone does not establish who actually acted.

cardVisual.title: Risk connects likelihood to impact
cardVisual.caption: Prioritize treatment by considering how likely a scenario is and how much harm it could cause.

blocks.title: From scenario to treatment
blocks.caption: A treatment decision depends on a defined scenario and the organization's risk criteria.

items.label: Threat and vulnerability
items.detail: What could happen, and through which weakness?

items.label: Likelihood and impact
items.detail: Estimate the chance and consequence using defined scales.

items.label: Treatment
items.detail: Accept, avoid, transfer, or reduce within risk appetite.

blocks.title: Controls change the exposure
blocks.caption: Treatment should be monitored because controls, threats, and business impact can change.

items.label: Control
items.detail: A safeguard reduces likelihood, impact, or both.

items.label: Residual risk
items.detail: Remaining exposure is accepted or treated further.

blocks.prompt: Which pair is central to a simple risk estimate?
blocks.explanation: Likelihood describes how plausible the scenario is; impact describes the harm if it occurs.
blocks.hint: One dimension is chance and the other is consequence.

blocks.prompt: Why must risk criteria be defined rather than implied?
options: Different people need a consistent basis for comparing and treating scenarios
blocks.explanation: Defined scales, assumptions, and appetite make decisions consistent and explainable without pretending to remove uncertainty.
blocks.hint: Think about two teams making comparable decisions.

blocks.prompt: What is residual risk?
options: Exposure that remains after controls are applied
A list of all available safeguards
Risk that can never be reviewed
blocks.explanation: A control changes exposure but does not guarantee zero risk; the remaining exposure is residual risk.
blocks.hint: Residual means what is left.

leadVisual.title: Likelihood and impact work together.
leadVisual.prompt: What happens if an exposed admin account controls a critical system?
leadVisual.caption: This simple scale teaches the relationship; a real assessment also needs threat context, safeguards, and defined impact criteria.

cardVisual.title: Classify by consequence
cardVisual.caption: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability describe different harms and drive proportionate handling.

items.label: Availability
items.detail: Harm from disruption or loss of access

blocks.title: The same asset can need different protections
blocks.caption: Classify the consequence of disclosure, alteration, and disruption separately before selecting safeguards.

items.label: Confidentiality
items.detail: Would exposure harm people, operations, or trust?

items.label: Integrity
items.detail: Would an incorrect change cause harm?

items.label: Availability
items.detail: Would an outage prevent a critical activity?

blocks.title: From classification to handling
blocks.caption: A label is useful only when it changes handling, ownership, and review.

items.label: Label
items.detail: Record the sensitivity or criticality and rationale.

items.label: Handling rule
items.detail: Set access, encryption, retention, backup, or continuity controls.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Reassess when use, context, or consequence changes.

blocks.prompt: A public website has no private customer data but must not be altered. Which lens is especially important?
blocks.explanation: Public information may have low confidentiality needs while unauthorized alteration could damage trust or operations, making integrity important.
blocks.hint: Focus on harm from a false or changed page.

blocks.prompt: Why should classification consider the consequence of disruption?
options: Availability needs may drive continuity and recovery controls
Availability is the same as confidentiality
blocks.explanation: An outage can prevent a critical activity even when the information is not secret, so availability consequences influence safeguards.
blocks.hint: Ask what happens when users cannot reach the asset.

blocks.prompt: What makes a classification program useful after assigning a label?
options: The label changes handling and is reviewed when consequences change
The label is hidden from every custodian
The label grants every administrator access
The label never needs an owner
blocks.explanation: Classification connects consequence to handling rules and ownership; it should be revisited as context changes.
blocks.hint: A label must lead to a control.

leadVisual.title: Three lenses on the same information
leadVisual.caption: A public website can have low confidentiality needs and high integrity or availability needs.
